appraisal_events.evidence: « je sentis s'opérer en moi une miraculeuse désincarnation ; elle se doubla aussitôt de la vague envie de vomir... on dut me mettre au lit avec une fièvre si tenace, que le docteur déclara qu'il fallait renoncer non seulement à me laisser partir maintenant à Florence et à Venise » ; « Et hélas, il défendit aussi d'une façon absolue qu'on me laissât aller au théâtre entendre la Berma » ; « Aller aux Champs-Élysées me fut insupportable. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's ecstatic anticipation of Venice and Florence collapses by bathos into nausea, fever, and a medical interdiction that strips him of travel, of la Berma, and of every source of exaltation, leaving him supervised on a public lawn. The self-ironizing deflation reinforces rather than softens the diminishment.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ce nom de Gilberte passa près de moi... formant, passager céleste au milieu des enfants et des bonnes, un petit nuage d'une couleur précieuse... quelque apparition de la vie des dieux » ; « si familier et si maniable pour cette fille heureuse qui m'en frôlait, sans que j'y pusse pénétrer »
appraisal_events.explanation: The cry of her name transfigures Gilberte into a quasi-divine apparition whose daily intimacy constitutes a valued world the narrator can brush against but not enter; the same movement that raises her marks his exclusion and dependence.

status_effects.explanation: He loses everything he had built his exaltation upon and then finds himself painfully outside Gilberte's life, his moods thereafter governed by whether she deigns to appear.
He is shut out of the intimate circle the name evokes; his later admission to the game of barres is conditional, prompted by a shortage of players, and repeatedly cancelled by her absences.
The passage raises her to the level of a Poussin sky and an apparition of the gods, making her the luminous centre of the episode.
She gains leverage over the narrator: he waits, circles the lawn, and takes her casual « J'espère bien que non ! » as a wound, while she treats her own absences as natural.

ambiguities: The closing turn — Gilberte having him asked to complete her camp, after which « je jouai désormais avec elle chaque fois qu'elle était là » — could be read as realized inclusion and a positive reversal. Read here as subordinate: the invitation is functional (they lacked players), and the passage immediately dissolves it into her absences and indifference, so the dominant movement remains deprivation and exclusion rather than renewal.

Gilberte's elevation attaches to the aura of her name as the narrator's imagination charges it, not to any social judgment of her by others; whether the retrospective narrator endorses this mythologizing or exhibits it as a youthful error is left open, though the lyric commitment of the sentence supports reading the elevation as endorsed at the local level.
